newsitem.title: USA: Teamster chief rises early to fend off challenge.
newsitem.headline: Teamster chief rises early to fend off challenge.

text.p: Teamsters go to work early. And if Ron Carey wants to keep his job as head of their union, he has to start early too.

At 6 a.m. one day recently, the president of the powerful International Brotherhood of Teamsters greeted workers at a Pepsi-Cola bottling plant in northern New Jersey, pressing his campaign themes of reforming and rebuilding the union.
Glad-handing and back-slapping his constituents for votes, Carey is doing his best to fend off a determined challenger.

When time permits, he tells them that his five-year effort to clean up the union, organise more workers and find new ways to battle hostile employers is working. Often he just listens. Always, he urges them to take responsibility for their union.
"You have to get involved in the union," he admonishes. "It's your union. It's not ours."
Campaigning is an ordeal that past presidents of what was once America's biggest labour union -- it's now No. 2 -- did not have to endure. They were elected by convention delegates.

But a 1989 settlement of a federal racketeering suit changed all that. The union that for years symbolised labour corruption agreed to choose its leaders in government-supervised elections open to the rank-and-file.

Early next month 1.4 million Teamsters will receive ballots in the mail asking them to choose between a slate headed by Carey and one headed by his bitter rival, James Hoffa Jr., the son and namesake of Carey's most notorious predecessor.
Both are crisscrossing the country, speaking at rallies and greeting workers at plant gates and truck barns.

Carey, 60, who won his office in a three-way race in 1991, says his polls have him comfortably ahead in the current rough-and-tumble campaign, even though Hoffa is outspending him by more than two-to-one. But the mud has been flying.

Hoffa's forces have accused Carey of owning $2 million of closely held stock in United Parcel Service, the largest Teamster employer, and of using a UPS lawyer to help swindle an old lady out of more than $300,000. Carey has responded by filing a libel suit against Hoffa and his allies.

Carey claims Hoffa's "Old Guard" supporters smeared him well before Hoffa entered the race last year by planting stories in the press that alleged Carey had shady real estate dealings and had ties to a mobster 20 years ago. Government overseers, who have broad investigative powers under the 1989 racketeering settlement, found no significant improprieties.
Carey, who calls his 55-year-old opponent "Junior," stops just short of accusing Hoffa of being backed by the mob.
"His view is to go back to the weakness and corruption of the past," he said. "You've got to think about what's in it for employers, what's in it for the mob, what's in it for Junior?"

If there is a philosophical difference in the race it is that Carey wants a prominent role for the union's Washington headquarters, while Hoffa wants to stop funding some of its programmes, funnel the savings into the union's depleted strike fund and have less oversight over the union's 600 locals.

Carey has enlarged the staff of the Teamsters' "Marble Palace" headquarters while still managing to cut its payroll. He beefed up spending for organising, training and research and created a "strategic campaigns" office that devises innovative tactics to use against employers during disputes.
When he took over, he sold the union's jet and cut his own salary. Last year, he ended 16 years of declining membership and 11 years of deficit spending.
"What we're doing is working. People are beginning to see the change and there's a confidence building," he said.

But the three-week nationwide truck strike he led in 1994 depleted the strike fund and members rejected his proposed dues hike to fortify it. Also, by eliminating a layer of unelected regional Teamster bureaucracy for an $11 million savings and by putting 66 locals under temporary trusteeships, mostly because of corruption, Carey has angered many of his members.
Then there were the Pepsi workers. Some, upset about a concession their local accepted in May, said they should have gone on strike. But Carey counselled restraint.
"They've got enough power to bury us," he told the workers. "We have to try to build a national agreement."
Later that morning, Carey went to a UPS facility in nearby Edison, N.J., greeting workers as they changed shifts. It was a friendly crowd. After all, he was once one of them.

A former marine, Carey worked for UPS for 11 years until he was elected president of Local 804 in Queens, N.Y., in 1967. There he mainly represented UPS workers and was known as a dissident before his upset win as general president in 1991.
Carey's next stop was an Anheuser-Busch brewery in Newark, N.J., where some of the workers belong to a local that backs Hoffa.
"We respect Mr. Carey, but we think we need something stronger," said employee Richard Lizak as several of his co-workers in the company cafeteria nodded in agreement.
Carey admits it can be tough running against the Hoffa name and the glory days it conjures up for some Teamsters. But he writes it off to selective memory and is undeterred.
"Sure, it has a bit of glamour," he said. "But I think after people think about it, he's just an empty suit."
